title: The ORCHID Index: Development, Content Validation, and Pilot Testing of a Composite Instrument Integrating Oral Disease Burden into Cardiovascular Risk Stratification to Advance Interdisciplinary Noncommunicable Disease Prevention
content: Background/Objectives: Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death in India, where the cardiometabolic burden is immense and periodontitis affects roughly half of adults. Although consensus statements from the American Heart Association and the European Federation of Periodontology confirm an independent association between periodontitis and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, no established cardiovascular risk instrument incorporates oral parameters, and dental and medical screening remain largely siloed. This study aimed to develop, validate for content, and pilot test the ORCHID Index, a rapid single-page composite instrument integrating oral disease burden with cardiometabolic and lifestyle risk into one thirty-point score, and to evaluate its content validity, internal consistency, inter-rater reliability, structural validity, and field feasibility. Methods: Development followed COSMIN-informed measurement standards across three phases. Three predefined domains were populated with items scored zero to two, a multidisciplinary expert panel established content validity, and a cross-sectional pilot of one hundred adults attending dental and primary-care settings in Navi Mumbai applied the tool, with cardiometabolic values abstracted from available clinical records rather than newly measured. Reliability, confirmatory factor analysis, and feasibility were assessed. Results: The final instrument contained fifteen items across three domains. The scale-level content validity index was 0.92, Cronbach’s alpha 0.8/, the inter-rater intraclass correlation 0.91, and the three-factor model showed good fit (comparative fit index 0.96). Mean completion time was 4.3 minutes, data capture 96 percent, and clinician usability 91 percent. Scores were higher among participants with severe periodontitis and documented cardiometabolic disease. Conclusions: The ORCHID Index is a feasible, content-valid, and reliable composite tool that operationalises the mouth-to-heart link at the point of care and aligns with global and national policy directions integrating oral health into noncommunicable disease prevention. Predictive validation in longitudinal research is the priority next step.
